content: Levonorgestrel is an oral emergency contraceptive approved by the FDA for the prevention of pregnancy following unprotected intercourse or suspected contraceptive failure. For optimal effectiveness, the tablet should be taken as soon as possible within 72 hours of intercourse. Common side effects include menstrual bleeding, nausea, lower abdominal pain, fatigue, headache, and dizziness. Adult Indications and Dosage FDA-Labeled Indications and Dosage (Adult): Levonorgestrel should be taken orally as soon as possible within 72 hours after unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure. The efficacy is higher when taken promptly. The standard dose is 1.5 mg of levonorgestrel. Off-Label Use and Dosage (Adult): Limited information is available regarding off-label guideline-supported or non-guideline-supported use of levonorgestrel in adults. Pediatric Indications and Dosage FDA-Labeled Indications and Dosage (Pediatric): There is limited information regarding FDA-labeled indications and dosage for pediatric use. Off-Label Use and Dosage (Pediatric): Limited information is available regarding off-label guideline-supported or non-guideline-supported use in pediatric patients. Contraindications Levonorgestrel is contraindicated in cases of known or suspected pregnancy. Warnings Ectopic pregnancies account for approximately 2% of all reported pregnancies. Up to 10% of pregnancies reported in clinical studies of progestin-only contraceptives are ectopic. A history of ectopic pregnancy is not a contraindication for levonorgestrel use, but healthcare providers should consider the possibility of ectopic pregnancy in women who become pregnant or report lower abdominal pain after taking levonorgestrel. Levonorgestrel is not effective in terminating an existing pregnancy. Spotting may occur a few days after taking levonorgestrel. Menstrual bleeding patterns may be irregular among women using progestin-only oral contraceptives or levonorgestrel for emergency contraception. If menstruation is delayed by more than one week, pregnancy should be considered. Levonorgestrel does not protect against HIV infection (AIDS) or other sexually transmitted infections (STIs). A physical examination is not required before prescribing levonorgestrel. However, a follow-up physical or pelvic examination is recommended if there are concerns about the general health or pregnancy status of a woman after taking levonorgestrel. Fertility is likely to return rapidly after treatment with levonorgestrel for emergency contraception. Routine contraception should be continued or initiated as soon as possible to ensure ongoing pregnancy prevention. Levonorgestrel contains FD&C Yellow 6 as a color additive. Adverse Reactions Common adverse reactions reported in clinical trials include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, dizziness, headache, dysmenorrhea, irregular menstruation, oligomenorrhea, and pelvic pain. Drug Interactions Drugs or herbal products that induce enzymes, including CYP3A4, which metabolize progestins, may decrease the plasma concentrations of progestins and reduce the effectiveness of progestin-only pills. Examples include barbiturates, bosentan, carbamazepine, felbamate, griseofulvin, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, rifampin, St. John’s wort, and topiramate. Significant changes in plasma levels of progestins have been noted in some cases of coadministration with HIV protease inhibitors or non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors. Consult the labeling of all concurrently used drugs for further information about interactions with progestin-only pills or potential enzyme alterations. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: Levonorgestrel is classified as Pregnancy Category X by the FDA. Studies have found no harmful effects on fetal development associated with long-term use of contraceptive doses of oral progestins. However, levonorgestrel is not effective in terminating an existing pregnancy. Nursing Mothers: Progestin-only pills generally do not adversely affect breastfeeding performance or the health, growth, or development of the infant. Small amounts of progestins pass into breast milk, resulting in detectable steroid levels in infant plasma. Pediatric Use: Safety and efficacy of progestin-only pills for long-term contraception have been established in women of reproductive age. Use of levonorgestrel emergency contraception before menarche is not indicated. Geriatric Use: This product is not intended for use in postmenopausal women. Race: No formal studies have evaluated the effect of race on levonorgestrel efficacy. A non-statistically significant increased rate of pregnancy was observed among Chinese women in clinical trials, but the reason for this is unknown. Renal and Hepatic Impairment: No formal studies have been conducted to evaluate the effect of renal or hepatic disease on the disposition of levonorgestrel. Immunocompromised Patients: There is no FDA guidance on the use of levonorgestrel in immunocompromised patients. Administration and Monitoring Administration: Limited information is available regarding administration in the drug label. Monitoring: Limited information is available regarding monitoring in the drug label. Overdosage There are no data on levonorgestrel overdose. However, nausea and associated vomiting may be anticipated as common adverse events. Pharmacology Mechanism of Action: Levonorgestrel acts as an emergency contraceptive primarily by preventing ovulation or fertilization (by altering tubal transport of sperm and/or ova). It may also inhibit implantation by altering the endometrium. It is not effective once the process of implantation has begun. Pharmacokinetics: Levonorgestrel is absorbed and metabolized in the liver. It is primarily excreted as glucuronide conjugates in urine (45%) and feces (32%). Metabolic clearance rates vary among individuals, contributing to variability in levonorgestrel concentrations. Clinical Studies A double-blind, randomized, multinational study evaluated the efficacy and safety of levonorgestrel for emergency contraception. Among women receiving levonorgestrel tablets, 84% of expected pregnancies were prevented. Emergency contraceptives are less effective than routine contraception, as their failure rate accumulates with repeated use. Patient Counseling Information Take levonorgestrel as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure. If vomiting occurs within two hours of taking the tablet, contact a healthcare provider to discuss whether to take another dose. Seek medical attention if severe lower abdominal pain occurs 3 to 5 weeks after taking levonorgestrel to evaluate for ectopic pregnancy. Consider the possibility of pregnancy if menstruation is delayed by more than one week beyond the expected date. Do not use levonorgestrel as routine contraception. Levonorgestrel does not protect against HIV or other sexually transmitted infections. For women under 17 years of age, levonorgestrel is available only by prescription.
